title: A skin-origin intervention that prevents atopic dermatitis and the atopic march

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an intervention applied to infant skin that durably prevents both atopic dermatitis and at least one allergic disease outside the skin, such as food allergy or asthma. It could act through the skin barrier, cutaneous immune activity, or skin microbes; these are candidate routes, not demonstrated solutions. The defining achievement would be prevention extending beyond eczema itself.

The biological rationale is that abnormal skin barrier function and inflammation might help initiate systemic allergic responses. Early atopic dermatitis is associated with food allergy and asthma, but that association does not establish that skin disease causes every later allergic outcome. Here, preventing the atopic march means demonstrating fewer cases of specified extracutaneous allergic diseases after a skin intervention, rather than assuming that all affected children follow one inevitable sequence. The supplied trials do not demonstrate this combined preventive capability.

significance.text: If demonstrated, this would give dermatology a primary-prevention capability extending beyond skin disease. The direct benefit would be fewer children developing atopic dermatitis and the particular extracutaneous disease or diseases shown to decline in trials. Establishing that an intervention beginning at the skin can change later allergic outcomes would also provide stronger evidence for a clinically actionable connection between cutaneous biology and systemic allergy.

Conditional impact synthesis: broader prevention of allergic disease would depend on how frequently disease begins through a modifiable skin pathway, which populations benefit, how long protection lasts, and whether families can use the intervention safely and consistently. The supplied evidence does not support a numerical estimate of the share of allergic disease that could be prevented. Success against one extracutaneous outcome would establish that specific benefit; it would not establish prevention of every manifestation of the atopic march.

The existing emollient findings illustrate an important limit on the proposed impact: lowering eczema incidence does not by itself demonstrate prevention of systemic allergy. CASCADE reported an atopic dermatitis benefit at age two while leaving the question of later allergic comorbidities open. BEEP did not demonstrate the combined preventive outcome through age five. These findings constrain claims about the tested regimens without ruling out other skin interventions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the supplied evidence is a causal, scalable skin intervention that durably lowers the incidence of both atopic dermatitis and at least one extracutaneous allergic disease. Daily emollients provide a biologically grounded test of barrier protection, but the reports give different results for eczema and do not establish the combined outcome. They therefore do not identify a sufficient preventive lever, and they cannot establish that every barrier, immune, or microbial approach has failed.

Scientific synthesis: a successful approach must identify which change in infant skin can alter subsequent disease development, when that change must occur, and in whom it matters. Improving a barrier measurement or reducing visible inflammation would be insufficient unless those changes translate into fewer clinical cases. A further challenge is separating a causal skin pathway from shared predispositions that could produce both eczema and extracutaneous allergy. Measuring a skin mediator can support this investigation, but measurement alone cannot establish that the mediator explains the clinical effect.

Engineering and implementation synthesis: the intervention must deliver a reproducible biological effect under infant-care conditions, with acceptable safety, adherence, cost, and delivery burden. Its formulation or other mode of delivery, treatment schedule, duration, and population boundaries would need definition. A regimen that works only with intensive trial support would leave scalability unresolved, even if its efficacy were convincing.

current_state.text: The Barrier Enhancement for Eczema Prevention trial, BEEP, randomized 1,394 term infants with a family history of atopic disease. Its five-year report found no preventive benefit from daily emollient application during the first year of life for atopic dermatitis, food allergy, asthma, or hay fever. The randomized enrollment should not be confused with the number providing each follow-up outcome. Follow-up used parental questionnaires, and cumulative parent-reported doctor-diagnosed food allergy was 92 of 609 children in the emollient group, approximately 15%, versus 87 of 632 controls, approximately 14%. These findings concern the tested regimen and population.

The supplied review assessed BEEP through a repository abstract and bibliographic record, not the full paper. That material supports the reported enrollment, questionnaire ascertainment, food-allergy counts, and overall conclusion, but permits only a limited methodological appraisal. The research notes cite Bradshaw and colleagues in Allergy as 2023, DOI 10.1111/all.15555, while the reviewed repository record gives an online publication date of 19 October 2022. The precise relationship between those bibliographic dates remains unresolved in the supplied material; it does not undermine the reported trial findings.

CASCADE, reported by Simpson and colleagues in JAMA Dermatology on 23 July 2025, DOI 10.1001/jamadermatol.2025.2357, enrolled infants without selecting them for elevated atopic risk. Physician-diagnosed atopic dermatitis recorded in health records by 24 months occurred in 36.1% of the daily-moisturizer group and 43.0% of controls. The reported relative risk was 0.84, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.73–0.97 and P=.02. This corresponds to a 16% relative reduction and a 6.9 percentage-point absolute difference. Those quantities describe the observed eczema benefit more precisely than calling it simply small.

CASCADE did not establish prevention of food allergy or asthma. Its food-allergy comparison was not statistically significant and lacked formal food-allergy testing; that limits inference about prevention rather than proving that no food-allergy effect exists. The article calls for longer follow-up to determine whether reduced atopic dermatitis translates into fewer allergic comorbidities. The BEEP and CASCADE results should therefore remain tied to their respective populations, regimens, follow-up periods, and outcome ascertainment.

The supplied review retained CASCADE's main article text, but did not inspect linked supplements or figure images. That text includes a January 2026 correction notice concerning the byline and Figures 3 and 4; the reviewed numerical conclusions above rely on retained prose. These are published trial reports, not projections or preprints. Together they document partial progress and limitations, without demonstrating durable prevention of both skin and extracutaneous disease. Because the supplied freshness search record is empty, they do not establish whether another intervention had achieved that capability by 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed efficacy demonstration: a preregistered randomized trial in infants should be adequately powered for both clinical atopic dermatitis and at least one prespecified extracutaneous endpoint, such as physician-diagnosed food allergy or asthma. It should show a prespecified, clinically substantial reduction in both outcomes, with follow-up through school age to establish durability. Effect thresholds, diagnostic methods, analysis plans, and handling of missing outcomes should be specified before results are known. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established consensus standards. An eczema-only benefit would not meet the combined target.
completion_criteria.label: Clinically substantial dermatitis and extracutaneous allergy reductions through school-age follow-up

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic demonstration: prespecified measurements should test the relevant skin pathway, supported by causal mediation analysis with its assumptions and limitations stated. A randomized clinical benefit would demonstrate the intervention's preventive effect; demonstrating that a particular skin mediator explains that effect requires additional causal reasoning. Correlation between mediator improvement and better outcomes would not, by itself, settle that mechanism.
completion_criteria.label: Skin pathway mediation assessed with stated causal assumptions and limitations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical demonstration: independent trials or independent replication across sites should confirm the combined benefit, with safety surveillance, adherence measurements, cost assessment, and delivery under routine-care conditions. Follow-up should clarify whether protection persists after treatment ends or requires continued use. Results should identify the ages, risk groups, populations, and allergic outcomes for which benefit is demonstrated. Finite trials establish those boundaries and the breadth tested; they cannot establish literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication confirms combined benefit and routine-care feasibility

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: DER-03, Antigen-selective erasure of pathogenic cutaneous immune memory, overlaps with DER-07 through cutaneous immune mechanisms. DER-07 is defined by preventing disease onset and later extracutaneous outcomes, whereas DER-03 is defined by selectively erasing pathogenic immune memory. The supplied roster does not establish that DER-03 cures atopic dermatitis, so that earlier comparison cannot be treated as a demonstrated capability.

Roster-based comparison: DER-04, Programmable passage of macromolecules and gene editors across intact stratum corneum, could conceivably supply a delivery method for a future DER-07 intervention. Passage across the barrier would not itself establish prevention. DER-02, One-time genomic cure of severe monogenic skin disease through the epidermal stem-cell compartment, also concerns durable changes originating in skin, but targets a genomic cure for severe monogenic disease. DER-07 specifies preventive clinical outcomes without requiring genomic editing or a one-time treatment.

Roster-based comparison: DER-01, Clinical restoration of a complete human skin organ; DER-08, Reconstitution of melanocyte stem cells where the follicular reservoir is gone; DER-09, Durable regenerative closure of diabetic foot ulcers after ischemia and pressure are treated; and DER-10, In situ reversal of established keloids and pathological cutaneous scars, concern restoring, reconstituting, closing, or remodeling damaged tissue. DER-07 instead seeks to prevent atopic disease before onset. A tissue-restoration achievement would require separate evidence to establish the combined allergic-disease prevention target.

Roster-based comparison: DER-05, Epidermal DNA repair sufficient to prevent ultraviolet-driven skin cancer, shares the objective of preventing disease through an intervention in skin, but addresses ultraviolet-driven carcinogenesis. DER-06, Therapeutic reset of the mutant epidermal field, concerns mutant epidermal tissue. Neither title establishes the barrier, immune, or microbial capability needed for DER-07, and their endpoints remain distinct.

Scope synthesis: DER-07 also overlaps with allergy, immunology, and pediatrics because its intended benefits extend to food allergy and respiratory disease during childhood. Oral allergen exposure was raised in the research as a contrasting prevention route, but the supplied evidence does not establish its efficacy or comparative scope. It remains a conceptual distinction between intervention routes, not an evidence-backed comparison in this record.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not establish whether another intervention achieved combined durable prevention by 1 November 2026; the freshness search record is empty.
Which skin pathway, intervention window, and infant populations could support prevention of both atopic dermatitis and extracutaneous disease remains unresolved.
CASCADE's longer-term effects on food allergy, asthma, and other allergic comorbidities are not established by the supplied report.
The intervention, disease-specific effect thresholds, diagnostic protocols, treatment duration, and implementation boundaries for a definitive demonstration remain to be specified.
The relationship between BEEP's reported 19 October 2022 online publication date and the research notes' 2023 citation remains unresolved.

BEEP's full paper and CASCADE's linked supplements and figure images were not assessed in the supplied review; the implications of the January 2026 CASCADE figure corrections cannot be independently resolved from this record.
The supplied evidence does not establish the efficacy of oral allergen prevention or a curative role for DER-03, so neither comparison is presented as an established clinical fact.

brief.title: Preventing eczema and later allergies through baby skin
possible: Parents could use a treatment on their baby's skin to prevent eczema and at least one allergic disease elsewhere in the body, such as food allergy or asthma. The protection would last into childhood.
why: Fewer children would develop skin disease and the particular allergy the treatment prevents. Doctors would also gain a way to prevent allergic disease by acting on the skin, strengthening the case that changes in skin can help drive allergy elsewhere.

sources.showed: BEEP found that daily moisturizer in infancy did not prevent eczema, food allergy, asthma or hay fever in children with a family history of allergic disease. Follow-up relied on parents reporting diagnoses.
sources.quote: Daily emollient application during the first year of life does not prevent atopic dermatitis, food allergy, asthma or hay fever.
sources.cited_for: Protecting infant skin with the tested moisturizer routine did not prevent skin disease or allergies elsewhere.
sources.not_established: This result does not establish whether other skin treatments could prevent both eczema and allergic disease elsewhere.

sources.who: Eric L. Simpson and the CASCADE Consortium
sources.showed: CASCADE found less eczema with daily moisturizer in infants enrolled without selection for allergy risk.
sources.quote: In this randomized, pragmatic, decentralized clinical trial of 1247 infant-parent dyads, those who were assigned to the daily moisturizer group had a lower cumulative incidence of AD compared with the standard of care group.
sources.cited_for: Daily moisturizer can reduce eczema, called atopic dermatitis or AD, under some trial conditions.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish prevention of food allergy or asthma, or lasting protection against both eczema and another allergic disease.

shown: The trials have reached different results for eczema. CASCADE reported a 16% relative reduction, while BEEP found no preventive benefit. Neither demonstrated lasting prevention of both eczema and an allergic disease outside the skin.
missing: A skin treatment has yet to demonstrate lasting reductions in both eczema and a specified allergic disease elsewhere.
Researchers have yet to establish which change in infant skin causes the combined preventive effect.
Independent trials have yet to confirm combined protection with safe, affordable use that families can sustain in routine care.

milestones.label: Substantial prevention of eczema and allergy through school age
milestones.explanation: A randomized infant trial would have to show meaningful reductions in both diseases through school age, using diagnoses and success thresholds set beforehand. This would establish lasting combined protection.

milestones.label: Evidence explaining how the skin produces protection
milestones.explanation: Measurements and causal analysis would have to assess whether the targeted skin change explains protection, with assumptions and limits stated. This would help distinguish a causal pathway from changes that merely occur together.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation and practical use in routine care
milestones.explanation: Independent trials would have to confirm combined benefit, safety, adherence, cost and routine delivery, identifying who benefits and whether protection outlasts treatment. This would establish reproducibility and practical reach.

uncertain: Which skin pathway, treatment window and infant populations could support combined prevention remains unknown.
Whether CASCADE's eczema reduction leads to fewer later food allergies or asthma remains unresolved.
The size of benefit needed for success, diagnostic methods and treatment duration still need definition.

page.title: Skin-directed prevention of atopic dermatitis and food allergy
page.definition: An intervention started on infant skin before eczema develops lowers the risk of both eczema and clinically confirmed food allergy, with protection persisting after treatment into childhood. Atopic dermatitis is eczema, an itchy inflammatory skin disease. A positive skin-prick test shows sensitisation. Confirming food allergy also requires evidence of a reaction when the food is eaten, from a clinical history or a supervised oral food challenge.

goal.need: In an Australian cohort at age one, allergy to peanut, egg white or sesame affected one in five infants with eczema and one in 25 without it. Preventing moderate or severe eczema could spare families lost sleep and time spent treating inflamed skin. Preventing food allergy would also spare children reactions when they eat the food. Moisturizers can control eczema flares, and early feeding can prevent some food allergies. Whether preventing eczema itself prevents food allergy remains unproven.

completion.title: One infant skin regimen reduces both eczema and confirmed food allergy through the fifth birthday.
completion.criterion: In one randomized cohort enrolled before atopic dermatitis develops, a skin intervention stopped by age 12 months reduces cumulative clinically diagnosed atopic dermatitis and clinically confirmed food allergy through age 5 years versus usual skin care. Both outcomes are prespecified, and each relative risk has an upper 95% confidence limit below 1. Food allergy is confirmed using the PEBBLES framework of sensitisation, reaction history and oral food challenge when indicated.
completion.set_by: Atlas. No external body identified defines this five-year joint efficacy test.
completion.basis: PEBBLES defines clinical eczema and confirmed food allergy at 12 months and registers repeat assessment at four years. BEEP followed children through age five using parental reports of clinician diagnoses. The Atlas adopts the five-year horizon and requires clinical confirmation of food allergy, cessation of the assigned treatment by 12 months and a separate confidence limit below one for each outcome.

milestones.title: A candidate emollient shows no detected skin-barrier harm after 4 weeks in a controlled skin assay.
milestones.criterion: In volunteers with inactive atopic dermatitis, compare one forearm treated with two fingertip units of the candidate emollient twice daily for four weeks with the control forearm. Assess water loss through the skin, outer-layer integrity and hydration, surface pH and redness before and after treatment with the observer blinded. The qualitative BEEP selection criterion is no detected harm to underlying barrier function.
milestones.set_by: University of Nottingham BEEP investigators, preparatory emollient selection described in the 2017 protocol. This qualitative criterion concerns emollients.
milestones.threshold_quote: showed they are not associated with any harm to the skin barrier

milestones.title: A six-week neonatal emollient study measures adherence and adverse events.
milestones.criterion: Enroll infants aged 0–4 weeks with a first-degree family history of allergic disease. Assign daily application of the ceramide-dominant emollient for six weeks to the body except the hands and face. Record applications and adverse events in a daily diary and assess infants at the six-week follow-up.
milestones.set_by: PEBBLES investigators, neonatal phase I study registered as ACTRN12609000727246 and described in the 2012 report.
milestones.threshold_quote: daily application of EpiCeram™ for six weeks.

milestones.title: Emollient use begun by nine weeks reduces clinician-diagnosed eczema by 24 months at two-sided P < .05.
milestones.criterion: Compare daily full-body emollient begun by age nine weeks and continued through 24 months with the CASCADE control regimen. Use the cumulative incidence of clinician-diagnosed atopic dermatitis recorded in the medical record by 24 months. Require a relative risk below one and a two-sided Wald test with P < .05 in the intention-to-treat analysis.
milestones.set_by: CASCADE Consortium, registered trial NCT03409367, its 2020 protocol and the analysis described in its 2025 report.
milestones.threshold_quote: 2-sided Wald test at the .05 level of significance.

milestones.title: Skin care begun at two weeks reduces allergy to any of four foods at age three at the 5% level.
milestones.criterion: In a birth-randomized factorial trial, compare assignment to emollient baths and facial cream at least four days weekly from age two weeks to before nine months with no assigned skin intervention, accounting for the randomized food intervention and its interaction with skin care. Require a reduction at the 5% significance level in allergy to any of peanut, cow’s milk, wheat or egg at 36 months. Count definite or probable allergy adjudicated by the masked expert panel, using oral food challenge when warranted and feasible.
milestones.set_by: PreventADALL investigators, trial NCT02449850 and its prespecified food allergy analysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: All hypotheses were tested at the 5% significance level without adjusting for multiplicity.

milestones.title: One neonatal skin regimen reduces both eczema and confirmed food allergy by 12 months.
milestones.criterion: In infants with a first-degree family history of allergic disease, compare a neonatal skin regimen continued to six months with standard skin care. Assess eczema in the first 12 months by modified UK Working Party criteria or visible eczema on examination, and food allergy at 12 months by sensitisation testing, reaction history and oral food challenge when indicated. Require an upper 95% confidence limit below one for each relative risk.
milestones.set_by: Atlas. PEBBLES defines both clinical outcomes and the treatment schedule. No external joint efficacy threshold was identified for the two relative risks.

milestones.title: The original trial groups undergo repeat clinical assessment for eczema and food allergy at age four.
milestones.criterion: At four years, compare the original PEBBLES treatment and standard-care groups for both registered secondary outcomes. Assess eczema by UK Working Party criteria or blinded investigator examination. Assess food allergy using clinical history and sensitisation testing, with an oral food challenge offered for suspected allergy in sensitised children. This milestone requires an assessment of both outcomes by original assignment.
milestones.set_by: PEBBLES investigators, four-year observational follow-up registered under ACTRN12617001380381.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary and secondary outcomes are assessed again at the 4-year follow-up

not_found: No published phase III PEBBLES efficacy report was located.
No AAD or S3 guideline or BEEP, CASCADE, PEBBLES or PreventADALL protocol identified sets a five-year joint efficacy threshold for both clinical outcomes.

results.finding: BEEP's 5-year follow-up found a food-allergy adjusted RR of 1.11 among 1,241 children.
results.detail: This was a 5-year BEEP follow-up, not the 12-month PEBBLES endpoint. Eczema and parent-reported doctor-diagnosed food allergy were not reduced; the food-allergy confidence interval included 1.
results.quote: Although more parents in the emollient group reported food reactions in the previous year at 3 and 4 years, cumulative incidence of doctor-diagnosed food allergy by 5 years was similar between groups (92/609 [15%] emollients and 87/632 [14%] controls, adjusted relative risk 1.11, 95% confidence interval 0.84 to 1.45).

results.finding: Among 1,247 randomized CASCADE infant-parent dyads, daily emollient reduced clinician-diagnosed eczema by 24 months (RR 0.84).
results.detail: The paper reports 1,247 randomized dyads and lists 1,228 infants in the primary-outcome figure (603 moisturizer, 625 control).

results.finding: Doublebase gel showed no detected skin-barrier harm after 28 days in 18 adults with quiescent atopic dermatitis.
results.detail: Post-treatment measurements were taken 12–20 hours after the last application. The verdict rests on Doublebase gel.
